word_order: SOV — verbs/predicates consistently appear clause-finally, e.g. '수연이가 뭘 좋아하는지 모르는데' (object before verb '모르는데').
punctuation_present: sometimes — some sentences end with periods/question marks, others (especially trailing connective clauses) have none
register: spontaneous conversational speech (casual dialogue/interview transcript, includes disfluencies, self-corrections, trailing conjunctions)
non_boundary_traps: -는데 (often continues into next clause rather than ending)
그래서 at clause-medial position leading into next clause
trailing '그래서' with no following clause in transcript (sentence 1)
quotative '-다고/-냐고' before 하다/하니까 which attaches to following verb
target_language_risks: Korean SOV order means the verb (often carrying negation, tense, mood) appears only at the end, so early segmentation before the verb can produce mistranslated or incomplete English clauses lacking polarity or tense.
Zero pronoun/subject drop is common, so target English needs inferred subjects from prior context; splitting too early loses antecedent tracking.
Sentence-final speech-style endings (-야, -지, -네, -잖아) carry evidential/mood nuance not directly translatable without full clause.

Fragments ending in connectives like -는데, -니까, -고 look complete but are syntactically dependent on the next clause; translating them as standalone sentences in English creates unnatural or truncated meaning.
Frequent self-corrections and repetitions (매일, 매일, 매일) require holistic handling to avoid redundant literal repetition in English.
notes_for_prompt_writer: This is fast, informal spoken Korean with frequent clause-chaining via connective endings (-는데, -니까, -고, -면) that must NOT be treated as sentence boundaries; wait for the next finite predicate before segmenting. Discourse markers like 그래서, 근데, 그리고 typically open a new segment rather than close one, so segment after them, not before. Because Korean is head-final and pro-drop, delay segmentation until the main verb/predicate and any sentence-final particle (-요, -다, -네, -잖아) appear, since translating a fragment lacking the verb will misrepresent polarity, tense, or mood in English.
